Real-world scenario: a Hong Kong panel interview — STAR #3 in English, then small talk and a café order in Cantonese — plus reading a Tokyo street sign and a Seoul café menu. Hard cards first, then 2–3-day recap, then 10 light new cards, then the 15-question test. 先难后新，念出声。

tasks.prompt: STAR #3 timed take (2 min, aim 260–280 words): say S-T-A-R aloud, then answer one follow-up: 'How did you deal with missing data?' Record, listen back once, fix one phrase. Watch: defensible (di-FEN-si-bul), governance (GUV-er-nunss), took the initiative TO.
tasks.script:
S: On an AI data-centre policy research programme, I was the sole analyst. The scope was ambiguous: there was no agreed definition of an 'AI data centre', the public data on energy, water, cooling, cost and land use was fragmented and inconsistent, and the project direction changed quite often.
T: My task was to build a defensible evidence base and policy analysis for urban and governance questions, even though the requirements were unclear and I had no one to review my work.
A: First, I pushed for a working definition of what counts as an AI data centre, so the whole analysis was built on the same scope. Second, I mapped the data gaps. I counted which indicators Hong Kong was missing and compared them with other governments and regions. Third, because the direction kept shifting, I built an iterative research workflow, so I could update the analysis step by step without starting again. And after every meeting, I kept a written log of what we agreed: the direction, the deliverables and the deadlines.
R: As a result, I delivered a baseline analysis of data-centre governance mechanisms from an international perspective, plus a clear list of the data Hong Kong is still missing, which gives future policy work a starting point.
Looking back: I learned that in ambiguous projects, confirming the scope early and keeping a written record protects both quality and timelines. Next time, I'd also structure the questions as an issue tree from day one.
Follow-up (missing data, ~30 s): I treated the gaps as a finding. I counted which indicators Hong Kong was missing, compared them with other regions, and the gap list became one of the deliverables.

tasks.prompt: 60-second self-intro, no notes. Order: Present → Past → Future (现在→过去→未来). One method + one number.
tasks.script: I'm an urban analytics graduate from HKU, and I turn spatial data into decisions. Most recently, I worked as a research assistant on an ageing-friendly city project at HKU. I built street view image datasets of public housing estates with the government's CSDI API, Python and ArcGIS Pro, reaching about 98% coverage, and used a YOLO model with a precision of about 0.8 to detect older pedestrians. Going forward, I'm looking to apply spatial analysis to real planning decisions, and that's why this role interests me.

tasks.prompt: Tone pairs ×3 each: 事 si6 / 試 si3, then 合作 hap6 zok3. Then play the café scene both roles in one go: order, customise, ask the price, pay. Last, explain in one breath why 事 and 試 sound different: point, reason, example.
tasks.script:
事 si6 (low, flat) / 試 si3 (mid, flat) ×3 · 合作 hap6 zok3 (low-short, then mid-short) ×3.
Café: 店員: 飲咩呀？ (jam2 me1 aa3? What to drink?) · 你: 唔該，一杯凍檸茶，走冰，少甜。 · 你: 幾多錢呀？ · 店員: 十八蚊。 (sap6 baat3 man1, $18) · 你: 可唔可以畀八達通？ · 店員: 得。 (dak1, OK)
Explanation: "事 and 試 have the same syllable but different tones. 事 is tone 6, low and flat, while 試 is tone 3, mid and flat. For example, 有咩事 uses the low one and 面試 uses the mid one."
